notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa008a.opp-l: Line 2: 'ei continendo habet et confitendo' is unclear; read as 'et continendo habet et confitendo' and the sense supplied in brackets is conjectural. Line 3: in 'Credo Deum' / 'credere illum' the distinction (believing that he exists, i.e. that he is God) is rendered with bracketed supplements; 'Jun credit' read as 'Qui credit', 'adhac' as 'adhuc', 'pedum pigri' as 'slow-footed'. Line 4: 'cdefacienie' read as 'calefaciente'; 'cur Virginis' as 'cor Virginis'; 'Irascendi' as 'nascendi'; 'Quod vero majestatis Deus de Mad;. incarnatus est' is an awkward, possibly corrupt sentence; 'Nec fuit Deo injuria causa misericordiæ' is obscure; final 'reticere' read as 'reficere' (remake), which the sense requires.

Many scanning errors corrected silently. Notable readings: 'Matth. XXVIII, 13' should be 28:18; '1 Cor. 1:23' should be 1:25. In ch. V 'memoriam sui in caelesti regno fieri a consorte supplicii precabatur' (thief begs his fellow-sufferer, i.e. Christ). In ch. VI 'legeretur' read as 'tegeretur' (covered), 'veumudatus' as 'venundatus' (sold), 'dæmonnaiauterret' as 'daemonum auferret' (conjectural); 'tentus' (seized) may be a dittography of 'tentatus'. The chapter VI heading oddly includes the sentence on burial. 'Ero mors na, o mora' read as 'Ero mors tua, o mors'.

Line 10: 'Ascendit ad coelos' — the Creed's ascension clause; the text's '(a)', '(b)' are editorial note marks and are omitted. Line 11: 'referat' rendered 'receive' (Vulgate sense of 2 Cor. 5:10). Line 12: 'ab auditu malo' echoes Ps. 111:7 (Vulg.), 'evil tidings'; kept literal. Line 14: 'Nihil majus aut minus' and 'Æqualitatem personarum dicit' read like comment on a quoted creed (Athanasian); 'I...' before 'Pater et Filius' is damaged, read as 'Ita'. The sentence on the assumed man is elliptical; bracketed words supply the contrast. 'vena' taken as an underground vein of water. Line 15: the Exodus reference is printed 'X!!, 46', evidently 12:46. The interpretation of Cyprian's sentence on light is obscure in the Latin ('lucem non capere divisionem, nisi in sanctis...'); translated literally. 'Sricendum' read as 'Sciendum'.

Line 16: 'in horis' read as 'in nobis' ('recognise in us something of their own virtues'); 'quod sicut mors illorum' taken as 'ut sicut'. Line 17: 'tantum pluit diabolus' read as 'tantum potuit'. Line 18: 'cognatio' read as 'cogitatio' ('thought'); 'domina tua' taken as 'dominae suae'; Psalm reference printed '2 et 5' should be 2–3; 'Et si non dubil' read as 'Et si non dabit'.

Line 19: the citation 'Isai. nIV' is garbled; the passage is Isa. 57:17–18. Line 21: 'Ecclus.' renders 'Eccli.' (Ecclesiasticus/Sirach). Line 22: the sentence 'Qua; demerserit, illa sibi eorum quo momentum vergitur, opcrarium vindicabit' is corrupt; it is translated by its evident sense (the heavier side of the scale claims the worker). The quotation 'Qui redit a justitia ad peccatum...' is from Ecclus. 26:27/28, not Proverbs, though the text places it before the Proverbs citation. The heading 'Caute legatur' ('Let this be read with caution') appears to be an editorial warning about the doctrine of weighing good and bad works.

nodes.text: SERMON
ON THE CREED.

INTRODUCTION. The necessity of inward and outward faith. The Creed is the rule of faith. On what principle it was established. What it contains. It is known to your Charity, dearly beloved, that soldiers of the world, when they are about to receive temporal benefits from temporal lords, are first bound by military oaths, and profess that they will keep faith with their lords. How much more, then, ought those who are about to serve as soldiers of the eternal King, and to receive eternal rewards, to be bound by heavenly sacraments, and publicly to profess the faith through which they are to please him? For the Apostle says, Without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6). This [faith] he recognises in our hearts who searches the reins and the hearts (Ps. 7:10). But for the sake of preserving the unity of the Church, under the dispensation of this present time, confession of the mouth is necessary together with faith of the heart: for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:10), not only for preachers but also for hearers. For otherwise a brother would not think well of a brother, nor would the peace of the Church be preserved, nor could anyone teach another, or learn from another, what is necessary for salvation, unless he transmitted what he has in his heart to the hearts of others by the signs of words, as by their vehicles. Faith, therefore, must both be kept in the heart and brought forth by the mouth. For faith is the foundation of all good things, and the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one will be able to come into the number of the sons of God: for without it a man neither obtains the grace of justification in this world, nor will he possess eternal life in the world to come. And if anyone has not walked by faith, he will not come to sight. Mindful of this, the holy Apostles handed down a sure rule of faith, which, comprised in twelve statements according to the number of the Apostles, they called the Creed (Symbolum): through it believers were to hold catholic unity, and through it they were to refute heretical depravity. Our forebears, then, have said that the Creed was established on the following principle.

For they relate that after the ascension of our Lord and Saviour to the Father, when his disciples, set on fire by the coming of the Holy Spirit, were speaking in the tongues of all [peoples], being about to go out to each and every nation to preach the word of God, and to depart from one another, they first settled in common a standard for their future preaching, so that, when they had gone away from one another to different places, they should not preach anything differing or discordant to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ. So, all being gathered in one place and filled with the Holy Spirit, they brought together a brief token of their preaching, each contributing what he held, and they established that this rule was to be given in this way to believers. The Creed is brief in words, but great in sacraments. For whatever was prefigured in the Patriarchs, whatever was announced in the Scriptures, whatever was foretold in the Prophets, whether concerning God unbegotten, or God born of God, or concerning the Holy Spirit, or concerning the receiving of every sacrament, or concerning the death of the Lord and the mystery of his resurrection, this Creed contains it all briefly, and by containing [it] holds [it] and by confessing [it professes it]. Let each one, therefore, who professed the apostolic faith in Baptism through the mouths of those who carried him, learn it when he has come to the years of understanding. Now let us come to the sacrament and the text of the profession of this Creed, which begins in this way:

CHAPTER ONE. To believe God, to believe God's word, to believe in God. The faith of the devil. Almighty. I believe in God the Father almighty. First of all, dearly beloved, attend carefully to what kind of saying stands at the head of the Creed. First, then, it has: I believe. See that our Lord does not command us to examine the divine judgements, but to believe; nor to seek out reasons, but to show faith simply and unshakeably. It does not say, I believe God [exists]; or, I believe God; although these too are necessary for salvation. For it is one thing to believe him, another to believe [that he is] he, another to believe in him. To believe him is to believe that the things he says are true; to believe [that he is] he is to believe that he himself is God; to believe in him is to love him. To believe that the things he says are true, many even of the wicked can do: for they believe them to be true, and are unwilling to make them their own, because they are slow-footed toward this. To believe that he himself is God, even the demons hold. But to believe in God only those know how to do who love him, who are Christians not only in name but also in deeds and in life, because without love faith is empty. With love it is the faith of a Christian; without love, the faith of a demon. Those, then, who are unwilling to believe Christ do not yet even imitate the demons. Whoever believes Christ but hates Christ has the confession of faith out of fear of punishment, not out of love of the crown: for they too were afraid of being punished. Indeed, when blessed Peter, confessing the Lord, said, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16), he seems to bring forth from his mouth almost the same words as the demons; but their confession, because it was uttered with hatred of Christ, was rightly condemned; his, because it came forth from inward love, was rewarded with eternal blessedness. Let us, then, who are sons of God through the adoption of grace (Rom. 8:15), in saying, I believe in God the Father almighty, mean this: let us so believe him as to cleave to him through love. In God the Father almighty. Notice that in joining the name of the Father to God in the confession, it shows that he did not begin to be God first and afterwards Father, but that without any beginning he is always both God and Father. When you hear Father, recognise that he has a Son truly begotten, just as one who possesses something is called a possessor, and one who rules over someone is called a lord. God the Father, then, is the name of a hidden sacrament, whose true Son is the Word. Nor let anyone ask how he begot the Son, which even the Angels do not know, and which is unknown to the Prophets. Hence that was said: Who shall declare his generation? (Isa. 53:8). Nor is God to be examined by us, but believed. But to put it briefly, it is enough for us to know that light begot radiance. It calls him almighty because he is almighty, he to whom nothing is impossible, who created heaven and earth, the sea, men, and all animals and creeping things, not by any act of labour, but by the sole command of his word. And therefore let it not come into our thoughts how this or that could have been done, since we are commanded to confess him almighty.

CHAPTER II. Jesus, Christ, Only. Christ compares himself to a worm on account of his conception. This manner of being born is neither an injury to God nor impossible. And in Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord. Notice that just as one must believe in the Father, so too in the Son. And since he is equal with the Father in majesty, we know that we owe to him as much honour and dutiful service as to the Father. Jesus, moreover, is interpreted Saviour. He is called Jesus because he saves the people. Christ is named from chrism: because just as the kings of old were anointed with sacred oil, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled with the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Only, because he admits neither comparison nor likeness with creatures, since he himself is the supreme creator of all things. Men are called sons of God through grace; he alone is the Son begotten by nature. These [titles] show that he is rightly to be believed in, who, because he is equal to the Father, is our Saviour redeeming us, and Christ the King ruling us, and our only Lord, who, having despoiled the ancient enemy, takes us into his own singular lordship. Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit: that is, of whose conception the Holy Spirit alone was the author. For just as a worm is formed from pure mud when the sun warms it, so, with the Holy Spirit enlightening and sanctifying the heart of the Virgin, the flesh of Christ was conceived from the flesh of the Virgin alone, with no seminal origin of flesh at work. Hence, comparing himself to a worm, he says through the Psalmist, I am a worm, and no man (Ps. 21:7): that is, not conceived in the human manner. Born of the Virgin Mary. He who came to renew human nature grown old in men's sins willed to have a new law of being born. The Only-begotten of God therefore became the son of man, so that he who was Creator of the world might become its Redeemer too. That the God of majesty was made flesh from Mary: he was not defiled by being born of a Virgin, who was not polluted when he fashioned man out of dust. Indeed, if the sun or fire touches mud, it purifies what it has touched, and yet does not soil itself. Nor was mercy's cause an injury to God. Nor let it be incredible that he was born of a Virgin, who could form Adam from virgin dust and the first woman from a rib. God gave his Son, whom alone he had begotten from his heart equal to himself and loved as himself, to Mary, so that by nature one and the same might be the common son of God and of Mary. All nature was created by God, and God was born of Mary. God created all things, and Mary bore God. God who made all things made himself from Mary, and thus remade all the things he had made. He who could make all things from nothing was unwilling to remake them, when they had been violated, without Mary.

CHAPTER III. Why the Lord willed to be crucified. The power of the cross. Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead and buried. This Pilate, under whom the Lord suffered, was the judge set over Judaea by the emperor at that time. Mention of him serves to mark the time, not to honour that person. Crucified. On this the Prophets foretold many things: how, crucified, he hung on the cross with outstretched hands in the sight of a wicked people. Yet, to put it briefly, he was hung on the cross to release us from the condemnation of the forbidden tree and to free us from death. But it is asked what the cross signifies, and why the Lord chose to suffer on the gibbet. To this a threefold reason is given. First, that Christ might be given as redemption for the guilt of the world, and the ancient enemy might be caught as if by the hook of the cross: that is, so that he might vomit up those whom he had swallowed, defeated not by power but by justice. The second reason is that he might offer to people who follow him a teaching for life. For he ascended the cross for this purpose, to offer us an example of passion and resurrection. The third reason for taking up the cross is that the pride of the world and its puffed-up wisdom might be humbled and fall through the preaching of the cross, foolish as it is thought, and might know that what is foolish of God is wiser than men. But we must still consider why the Lord chose such a kind of death. For we read in the Gospel that the Pharisees wanted to throw him headlong from the mountain, but he, passing through the midst of them, went his way (Luke 4:29-30). Elsewhere too we read that the Jews took up stones to throw at him, but he hid himself and went out of the temple (John 8:59). Why did the Lord not wish to be thrown headlong, or stoned, or even cut down with the sword? He certainly did this for the sake of our salvation. For the death of Christ is the sign of our salvation. So he did not wish to be stoned or struck with the sword, because, of course, we cannot always carry stones or iron with us to defend ourselves. But he chose the cross, which is traced by a light movement of the hand, and by which we are also fortified against the cunning of the enemy. For by this sign of the cross the Lord's Body is consecrated, the font of Baptism is sanctified, priests and the other ecclesiastical grades are ordained, and all things whatever that are sanctified are consecrated by this sign of the Lord's cross with the invocation of the name of Christ.

CHAPTER IV. The mystery of the cross. The depth of the mystery of the cross. For the cross itself also contains a great mystery in itself. Its arrangement is such that its upper part reaches toward the heavens, its lower part clings to the earth and, fixed there, touches the depths of the underworld, while its breadth reaches toward the parts of the world. For Christ too, through the passion of the cross, benefited the Angels in heaven, whose number, diminished through the apostate angel, is filled up daily from the souls of the faithful; and [benefited] us who are on earth, and those who were held in the underworld on account of original sin; and also those who lived in the various parts of the world. The cross lying flat reaches toward the four parts of the world, namely east and west, north and south, because Christ too through his passion draws all nations to himself and has subjugated all things to himself, as he himself says, rising from the dead: All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18). A higher sacrament also is contained in this figure of the cross, which deserves the more careful attention the higher it is. For in the breadth of the cross is understood love of neighbour, which is to be extended not only to friends but even to loving one's enemies. In its length, too, is understood the long and persevering endurance of toils and persecutions, which our pilgrimage, sighing for its homeland, must bear patiently, as much for love of neighbours as for the performance of all good works. By a similar relation, in its height is figured the loftiness of hope, which penetrates even within the veil, where those enjoy the vision of peace who here are tried in many ways by the citizens of Babylon, until they are freed from the slavery of this corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God. The depth of the cross must also be considered, because deep is the mystery of the cross, in which the wits of many who are called wise have failed: they dared to censure what they could not comprehend by human reason, namely why the Word, coeternal with God the Father, containing all things, filling all things, enclosed himself wholly in the man he assumed, and yet did not cease to rule, fill and contain the whole world.

CHAPTER V. Why Christ chose the punishment of the cross. Through the death of the flesh he merited for us a twofold resurrection. Let there be no shame for us, then, in the cross of Christ, since we have victory from his passion. For just as the eternal Son of God was born not for himself but for us, so the spotless Lamb of God suffered not for himself but for us. Who would not perceive it to be a wonderful mystery, where the one proclaimed as man is God, and where the same one announced as Lord is recorded as crucified? Nor did his being slain happen to him as something unthought of or unforeseen, since by the counsel of his divinity he took up man precisely so that he could be killed for man. He chose the punishment of the cross so that a baser penalty might prepare a loftier victory, and so that he who suffered for the good of all might die raised on high, as it were in the sight of the world; at the same time, so that those who saw him crucified might behold the wonders of the crucified. For the sudden darkness of the sun, the trembling of the earth, the splitting of rocks, the resurrection of the dead showed fully and abundantly the glory of the one suffering. And of what weight is that testimony, that the thief, crucified alongside him, begged his partner in punishment to remember him in the heavenly kingdom? Hence it is, dearly beloved, that we do not lament with sighs the mockery and insults that Christ endured, his cross and his death, but celebrate them with continual praises. The death of our Lord Jesus Christ was not in the soul but in the flesh alone; but our death is not only in the flesh but also in the soul: in the soul because of sin, in the flesh because of the penalty of sin. He, however, because he committed no sin and had none in his soul, did not die except in the flesh only, and this through the likeness of sinful flesh which he drew from Adam. Therefore his single death benefited our double death, and his single resurrection [benefited] the resurrection of soul and body. For his resurrection undid our two deaths and shaped our two resurrections. And not without reason did he lie one day and two nights in the tomb, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. For he came to us, who were held in the death of flesh and spirit, and bore his one death of the flesh and undid our two. For if he had taken on both himself, he would have freed us from neither.

CHAPTER VI. What Christ provided for us through his weaknesses. He was buried, so that for the consolation of the buried the earth too might receive the blessing of his body. The weak things of the incarnate Word are recalled, of which the Apostle says: What is weak of God is stronger than men (1 Cor. 1:25). He was born of a Virgin, so that we might be born of the womb of the virgin Church; he was tempted, so that he might free [us] from temptation; he was seized, so that we might be released; bound, so that we might be loosed from the knot of the curse; he was mocked, so that he might free us from the mockeries of demons; he was sold, so that he might redeem us; he was humbled, so that he might exalt us; he was taken captive, so that he might take us away from the captivity of demons; he was stripped, so that the nakedness of the first man, through which death entered, might be covered; he was crowned with thorns, so that he might free us from the thorns of sins, or rather so that he might show that he was to be crowned with them, and that those who were thorny by loving vices would become the head and crown of the Church; he was given vinegar to drink, so that he might inebriate us with the sweetness of heavenly desire and eternal joy; finally he was sacrificed on the altar of the cross, so that he might blot out the sins of the whole world; he died, so that he might take captive the dominion of death; he was buried, so that he might bless the burial of the saints, and so that he might bury us to vices and lusts for himself. This weakness of Christ, then, overcame all the strength of the world.

CHAPTER VII. What he did in hell. He descended into hell, so that he might free Adam the first-formed, and the Patriarchs, and the Prophets, and all the just who were held there on account of original sin; and so that he might call back those released from the chains of sin, redeemed by his blood from that same captivity and place of hell, to the heavenly homeland and to the joys of everlasting life. The rest, who beyond original sin committed a capital fault, as Scripture asserts, remained in the penal Tartarus, as was said through the prophet in the person of Christ: I will be your death, O death; that is, by his death Christ killed death, the enemy of the human race, and gave life. I will be your bite, O hell (Hos. 13:14). He bit hell in part, as regards those whom he freed; in part he left [it], as regards those who for capital crimes remained in torments.

The third day he rose again from the dead. If you have believed of Christ what is a matter of dishonour, believe what is a matter of glory. If you have believed what belongs to death, believe what belongs to life. For just as in the passion there is the mystery of mercy, so in the resurrection there is the working of power, as he himself says: I have power to lay down my life, and to take it up again (John 10:18). He ascended into the heavens: that is, he set the condition of our nature, which he took on when born of a human mother, above the heavens at the right hand of God the Father. Let us too ascend with Christ meanwhile in heart, so that when his promised day has come, we may follow in body also. Yet we ought to know, brothers, that pride does not ascend with Christ, nor avarice, nor lust; no vice of ours ascends with our physician. Therefore if we desire to ascend after the physician, we ought to lay aside vices or sins. For they all press upon us as if with fetters, and strive to bind us with the nets of sins; and therefore, with his help, according to what the Psalmist says, let us break their bonds (Ps. 2:3), so that we may be able to say securely to the Lord: You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice the offering of praise (Ps. 115:16–17). He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty. To sit belongs to one who judges. And because our Redeemer, taken up into heaven, both judges all things now and will come at the last as judge of all, he is described as sitting.

CHAPTER VIII. All people are to be judged by Christ. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. He will come to judgement in the very body in which he ascended into heaven, to judge Christians and pagans, the just and sinners, the faithful and the ungodly. For all of us, as the Apostle says, shall stand before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body, according as he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). This the Lord also announces in the Gospel, saying....

CHAPTER IX. How they ought to prepare themselves now for the last judgement. Let us chastise ourselves, let us render account to ourselves of our daily conduct, let us accuse ourselves daily to our judge; and while we are in the flesh, let us fight daily against that very flesh, with the Lord's help. Whoever does this will be freed from the evil hearing; but whoever scorns [it], what will he do on that fearful day of judgement, when, as the world trembles and the trumpets of the angels sound before, the Lord takes his seat on that throne of his majesty, surrounded by the light of the heavenly host....?

CHAPTER X. One must flee to the remedies of penance. The end should not always be delayed for the remedy of his salvation by one who is always uncertain of his life: for he who makes us secure by saying, On whatever day the sinner is converted, all his iniquities will be given over to oblivion (Ezek. 18:21–22), himself also wished us to be cautious, saying, Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day (Ecclus. 5:8). Let us therefore turn to better things while the remedies are in our power. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life by the merits of [our] life. Considering these things, then, most beloved brothers, wisely and faithfully, let us hasten to flee to the remedies of penance, and through chastity and humility, through works of justice and mercy, let us obtain for ourselves eternal things with God. But to return to the point from which we digressed, there follows in this holy Creed:

CHAPTER XI. The mystery of the Trinity is explained through likenesses. I believe in the Holy Spirit. Take note that as one must believe in the Father, so also in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not believe even in one person of the Trinity, it will not profit him to have believed in two. For this is the catholic faith: that we venerate, believe, worship and confess one God in Trinity, and Trinity in unity. And in this Trinity there is nothing before or after: for just as the Father was never without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, so also the Father and the Son were never without the Holy Spirit. The holy Trinity, then, is co-eternal, and an inseparable unity, without beginning and without end. Nothing greater or less. It speaks of the equality of the persons, because the holy Trinity is equal, and the deity is one, as the Apostle says and teaches: Through the things that have been made, [they] are understood and seen (Rom. 1:20), and the Creator is understood through the creature, according to these comparisons and very many others. The sun, brightness and heat: they are both three words and the three are one. What shines, this is hot; and what is hot, this shines: these three words are known as one thing. So the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, three persons, are one in deity, and are rightly believed to be an undivided unity. Again, from earthly things: a vein [of water], a spring, a river; these are three words, and the three are one in their nature: so the substance or deity of the three persons, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, is one. Neither the person of the Father nor that of the Holy Spirit, but only that of the Son, took on flesh. And so that you may understand this, I will use comparisons. Surely, so that you may understand the Creator from the creature: in the soul there is also reason; and though they are one, the soul does one thing, reason another; by the soul we live, by reason we are wise. So, although the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one substance, the whole Trinity made the man; [but] the one who assumed [him] was not the whole Trinity, but only the person of the Son. And although the Son of God himself was God and man, the man alone was subject to the passion. Just as, for example, we see a tree that has the splendour of the sun in it; and when it is cut, we see that the stroke of the striker's iron meets the splendour of the sun before the wood is reached; but the splendour, although it is there, can neither be cut nor separated by the hewer; so also the divinity can neither be separated nor cut: but that was subject to the passion which, like the wood, could be both bound and held. Therefore as in the Father and the Son, so also in the Holy Spirit we ought to believe. This, dearly beloved, is the unoffending rule of truth: that those whose being is one and who are one should not be separated by us on earth. For just as nothing among creatures can be made equal to the divinity, so the nature of the divinity excludes all division and inequality. For according to the truth of the Gospel, just as the Son came forth from the Father, so also the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; and just as the only-begotten Son is of God, so also the Holy Spirit is of God; and just as the Father has mercy on whom he will, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he will, so also the Holy Spirit is read both to inspire as he will and to distribute the gifts of heavenly graces as he will. Hence the grace of that same Spirit is rightly described by the prophet as sevenfold (Isa. 11:2–3); because indeed through his inspiration one comes to rest, and in the full perception and vision of him true rest is possessed. Of him it is rightly promised: He will teach you all things (John 14:26); because unless the same Spirit is present to the heart of the hearer, the teacher's speech is idle. Let no one attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher's mouth, for unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher's tongue labours outwardly in vain. Hence, since without him we can do nothing good, with his help let us make ourselves such that the Holy Spirit may deign to come to us and dwell in us.

CHAPTER XII. The Catholic Church. There are no greater riches than faith. The Church is one. The holy catholic Church. It must be known that we ought to believe the Church, but not believe in the Church: because the Church is not God, but the house of God. It says 'catholic', [meaning] spread through the whole world, because the churches of the various heretics are not called catholic for this reason, that they are confined to places and to their own several provinces. But this [Church] is spread from the rising of the sun to its setting with the splendour of one faith. There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honours, no greater wealth of this world than the catholic faith, which saves sinful men, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the just, crowns martyrs, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, prepares [them] for the heavenly kingdoms, and gives [them] a share in the eternal inheritance with the holy angels. Whoever he is, and whatever kind he is, he is not a Christian who is not in the Church of Christ. For she alone is the one through whom the Lord willingly accepts sacrifice, she alone intercedes confidently for those who go astray. Hence also the Lord gave a command concerning the offering of the Lamb, saying: In one house you shall eat [it], and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside (Exod. 12:46). For the lamb is eaten in one house, because the true offering of the Redeemer is sacrificed in the one catholic Church. The divine command forbids its flesh to be carried outside, because it forbids what is holy to be given to dogs. She alone is the one in which good work is done fruitfully; hence none received the wage of a denarius except those who had laboured within the vineyard. She alone guards those placed within her by the strong bond of charity. Hence also the water of the flood raised the ark to the heights, but destroyed all whom it found outside the ark. She alone is the one in which heavenly mysteries are truly contemplated. Hence the Lord says to Moses: There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock; and a little later: I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back parts (ibid. 33:21, 23). For because the truth is seen from the catholic Church alone, the Lord declares that there is a place with him from which he may be seen. Moses is placed on the rock so that he may contemplate the form of God; because unless one holds the solidity of the faith, he does not recognize the divine presence. Pluck a ray of the sun from its body, he says: the unity [of light] does not admit division of the light. Break a branch from the tree: once broken it cannot sprout. Cut off a stream from its source: once cut off it dries up. In these words of Cyprian we understand that the light does not admit division, except in the saints predestined to the kingdom of God, who can in no way be divided from the Church; and we take 'the broken branch does not sprout' [to refer to] the sprouting of eternal salvation. And the dryness of the stream cut off from its source we recognize in this: that those who are separated from the unity are emptied of the Holy Spirit.

CHAPTER XIII. Who may become a sharer in the merits of the saints. The communion of saints: that is, that we may be held in fellowship and in the communion of hope with those saints who died in this faith which we have received. If, then, we wish to have communion with the saints in eternal life, let us think about imitating them. For they ought to recognise in us something of their own virtues, so that they may deign to make supplication to the Lord for us. For if we cannot bear the torments which the saints endured, let us at least, with them interceding, fight against evil desires. For neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob was killed; and yet, honoured for the merits of faith and justice, they deserved to be the first among the Patriarchs. To their banquet is gathered whoever is found faithful and just and praiseworthy. Hence we too, dearest brothers, even if we suffer nothing of the kind, if we endure no chains, no scourging, no prisons, no other bodily punishments, no persecution from men for the sake of justice, shall nevertheless be able to obtain the fellowship of the saints, if we take care to chastise our body and bring it into subjection, if we accustom ourselves to make supplication to the Lord in a spirit of humility and with a contrite soul, if we strive to receive with a calm mind the insults inflicted by our neighbour, if we rejoice to love those who hold us in hatred and who do us injuries, to do good to them, and to pray for their life and safety, if we endeavour to be adorned, together with the virtue of patience, with the fruits of good works as well. For if we live in this way, and present our bodies, according to the Apostle's word, as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God (Rom. 12:1), we shall be granted by heavenly favour to be rewarded with a glory shared with those who gave their limbs to death for the Lord, so that, just as their death, so also our life may be precious in the sight of the Lord; and when the bonds of the flesh are broken, we too shall deserve to enter the courts of the heavenly city, and among the choirs of the blessed martyrs to render offerings of thanks to our Redeemer. These are the footprints which all the saints, returning to the homeland, left for us, so that, keeping to their paths, we might follow [them] to joy. Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland? A great number of dear ones awaits us there; a dense and copious crowd of parents, brothers, children longs for us, already secure about their own safety, still anxious about our salvation. To come into their embrace and sight, how great a joy is that for them and for us in common? There is the glorious choir of the Apostles. There is the illustrious number of the exulting Prophets. There the countless people of the martyrs is crowned for the victory of their contests. There the most radiant throng of virgins rejoices; there too the fortitude of the confessors is praised. And the reward of those too is assessed who, keeping the Lord's commandments, transferred their earthly patrimonies to heavenly treasuries. But what tongue is sufficient to tell, or what understanding to grasp, how great are those joys of the heavenly city: to be present among the choirs of Angels, to stand with the most blessed spirits before the glory of the Creator, to behold the face of God present, to see the uncircumscribed light, to be touched by no fear of death, to rejoice in the gift of perpetual incorruption? Let us hasten with eager longing to these elect of God, so that it may be our lot to be with them soon, and soon to come to Christ, to him whom we have as the leader of this journey, the author of salvation, the prince of light, the bestower of joy.

CHAPTER XIV. The remission of sins. The Novatians are refuted. The remission of sins. The remission of sins must above all be believed, brothers, because this is the one remedy which absolves the human race from the sentence of perpetual death. For this reason the Only-begotten of the Most High deigned to take on flesh and was content with the cross, so that pardon might make you innocent, who could not escape your crimes. For this reason the spotless Lamb was slain, so that by his blood the stain of the human race might be wiped away. But I wonder that some are so obstinate that they think penance should not be granted to the lapsed, or consider that pardon should be denied to penitents; since it is written, Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the former works (Apoc. 2:5). Certainly this is said to one who has evidently fallen, and whom the Lord exhorts to rise again through works, because it is written, Almsgiving frees from death (Tob. 4:11); and certainly not from that death which the blood of Christ extinguished once for all, and from which the grace of saving Baptism and of our Redeemer freed us, but from that which crept in afterwards through offences. For since it is written, The Lord did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living (Wisd. 1:13), certainly he who wishes no one to perish desires sinners to do penance, and through penance to return again to life. Therefore he also cries out through the prophet Joel and says, And now says the Lord your God: Return to me with your whole heart, and with fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments; and return to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and kind, and patient and of much compassion, and one who turns aside the sentence against the wickedness committed (Joel 2:12–13). The Lord too, showing in the Gospel the kindness of God the Father, says, Which man is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will hand him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he hand him a serpent? If therefore you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him (Matt. 7:9–11). Here the Lord compares a fleshly father and the eternal and generous kindness of God the Father. But if that worthless father on earth, gravely offended by a sinful and wicked son, nevertheless, if he later sees him reformed, and, having put away the offences of his former life, corrected by the sorrow of penance to sober and good ways and to the discipline of innocence, rejoices and gives thanks, and receiving him whom he had lost before, embraces him with the longing of a father's exultation: how much more does that one and true Father, good, merciful, kind, indeed goodness and mercy and kindness itself, rejoice in the penance of his children, and threaten neither anger nor punishment to those who repent, mourn and lament, but rather promise pardon and forgiveness? For if the devil could do so much as to lead you down from the lofty heights of virtues into the depth of evils, how much more will God be able to call you back to the highest peak of good things, and not only to call you back to what you were, but also to make you far more blessed than you seemed before?

CHAPTER XV. That one must not despair, and where despair comes from. One must not cease from praying for pardon. Only do not lose heart, and do not cut yourself off from the hope of good things; do not, I beg, let happen to you what usually happens to the impious. For it is not the multitude of sins that leads to despair, but impiety. And therefore Solomon did not say that everyone who comes into the depth of evils despises, but, The impious man, he says, when he comes into the depth of evils, despises (Prov. 18:3). It belongs to the impious, then, to despair of salvation and to despise, when they have come into the depth of evils, not [merely] of sins. For impiety does not allow them to look back to God and to return to the place from which they slipped away. This thought, then, which cuts off the hope of conversion, descends from impiety; and like a very heavy stone pressing on the neck of the soul, it always forces it to look downward to the earth, and does not allow it to lift its eyes to its God. But it belongs to a manly spirit and an excellent mind to throw off from the neck of its soul the hostile weight, indeed to cast away the devil who is pressing it down, and to command its soul to sing the prophetic words and say to the Lord, As the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes on the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we are greatly filled with contempt (Ps. 122:2–3). Truly excellent is the teaching, and of heavenly philosophy, in these words. We are filled, it says, with contempt: this is what it wished to teach us, that even if we are filled with the multitude of our sins, covered with contempt and reproaches, yet let our eyes be on the Lord our God until he has mercy on us. And let us not cease from entreaty before we deserve to obtain pardon of our sins. For this is the mark of a truly steadfast and persistent soul, that it is in no way driven back from perseverance in asking by despair of obtaining, but perseveres and persists in entreaties until he has mercy on it. And lest perhaps you think that you incur greater offence with God if, though you do not deserve to be heard, you persist importunately in prayers, remember the parable of the Gospel, and there you will find that the Lord does not show himself ungracious to persevering and importunate petitioners. For he says: And if he will not give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will rise and give him as much as he needs (Luke 11:8). Understand, therefore, dearest one, that the devil suggests despair of obtaining for this reason: to cut off from us the hope in God's goodness, which is the leader on the journey by which one goes to heaven. And just as in the case of common death it is philosophical to restrain oneself from tears, so in the death of the soul I consider it both foolish and irreligious to accept consolation.

CHAPTER XVI. However guilty people are, hope of life remains. God never spurns sincere penance. God created us for heaven, not for Gehenna. Through penance here sins of whatever size can be washed away. Indeed, I think we should be accused of sloth if, while those who mourn bodies and common death do this so harshly and so vehemently, though they know and are certain that their weeping is of no use for the life of the dead, we do nothing like this in lamenting for the soul, which we know can be restored to its former state through penance. For we know that many who slipped from the right road and were hurled down from entering the narrow way have been so restored again that their later state surpassed their earlier, and they reached the palm and the crown, and are believed to have been enrolled again in the number and choir of the saints. And I do not want you to think that my words concern only those who sinned in a few slight matters. I am speaking of the one who gave way to every evil, who by the enormity of his crimes shut himself off from the way to the kingdom of heaven; and who was not among the unbelievers but among the faithful, and among those who formerly pleased God but afterwards fell, whether into adulteries or into all the impurities which, as the Apostle says, it is shameful to speak of. For [God] never spurns penance if it is offered to him sincerely and simply: he takes it up, gladly accepts it, embraces it, does everything in order to call [the sinner] back to his former state. And what is still more excellent and outstanding: even if someone has not been able to complete the whole course of satisfaction, he still does not reject penance, however small and however briefly performed; he takes up even that, and does not allow the reward of a conversion to perish, however slight. For this is what Isaiah seems to me to indicate, where he says something like this about the people of the Jews: Because of sin I grieved you a little, and struck you, and turned my face away from you; and you were grieved, and you walked sorrowful, and I comforted you (Isa. 57:17–18). Having, then, these examples of penance, let us not persist in evils, nor despair of reconciliation, but let us say: Let us too return to the Father, and draw near to God. He will never, believe me, turn away from one who has turned to him. For he himself says: I am a God who draws near, and not a God from afar (Jer. 23:23). And again through the same prophet he says: Sins separate between me and you (Isa. 59:2). If, then, it is sins that separate us from God, let us remove this obstacle in the middle, and there is nothing to prevent us from being joined to God. For God created us, and made us exist who did not exist, for this purpose: to confer eternal good things on us and to grant us the kingdom of heaven. For he did not make us in order to hand us over to Gehenna and to everlasting fire. The kingdom of heaven was made for us, Gehenna for the devil. And let me show from the Gospels that this is so. For the Lord himself will say to those who will be at his right: Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you from the beginning of the world. But to those who will be at his left he will say: Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:34, 41). If, then, the Gehenna of fire was prepared for the devil, but the kingdom of heaven for man from the foundation of the world, all that matters is that we do not shut ourselves out from entering into good things by stubbornly persisting in evils. For while we are in this life, however great the sins that befall us, it is possible for all to be washed away through penance. But when we have been led away from this world, there, even if we repent (and we will repent greatly, but there will be no use in the penance), and though there be gnashing of teeth, though there be wailing and weeping, though we pour out prayers and cry out with countless entreaties, no one will hear, no one will help, nor will anyone pour water even with the tip of a finger on our tongue set in the flames; but we will hear what that rich man heard from Abraham: That a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, and no one can cross from here to there, nor from there to here (Luke 16:26).

CHAPTER XVII. Pleasures pass quickly. They lead to eternal torments. We enjoy them now as if in a dream. Let us therefore at last come to our senses, and remember what it profited those who remained in bodily luxury and the pleasures of the present life right up to their last day. Look now at their tombs, and see whether there is in them any trace of their boasting, whether you can recognise any signs of the luxury of riches. Ask now where the garments and foreign perfumes have gone, where the pleasure of the shows, where the crowds of followers, and the opulence of banquets; where laughter, jest, and unrestrained and unbridled merriment have gone, where they have departed. Where are those things now, and where are the people themselves? What is the end of both? Look more carefully, and come closer to the tombs of each. See only ashes, and the stinking remains of worms; and remember that this is the end of bodies, whether they spent their life in pleasures and merriment or in toil and continence. Now if every matter and every case came only as far as ashes and worms, these losses would be counted small, and such as the condition of nature could easily excuse. But now turn your eyes from these ashes and tombs, and call your thought back to that dreadful tribunal of divine judgement, which a burning river surrounds with flaming streams, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, where there is the outer darkness, where there is that worm of conscience which will never die, and the fire which will never be quenched. Remember the parable of Lazarus and that rich man who, [though] master of such great wealth, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, could not then find a single drop of water when he was placed in the extremity of burning. Tell me, I ask you, what more does this life hold than a dream? For just as those who are placed or condemned in the mines, or set in any other punishment, when perhaps after much hardship of life they have been relieved a little in sleep, see themselves placed among many dishes and enjoying most abundant feasts, but when they get up they find that nothing of pleasure has remained to them from the delight of the dream, so too that rich man had this life as a dream; when he departed, nothing remained with him but regret for the past and punishment for the present.

CHAPTER XVIII. Eternal punishments. The power of penance. Remember these things, and set that fire of Gehenna against these flames of lust and desire which now stir you up. This fire which is in the present life consumes everything it receives; but that one always torments those it has received, and keeps them always whole for its punishment. For this reason it is called unquenchable, not only because it is itself not quenched, but because it will not quench or destroy those it has received. For Scripture says that sinners too will put on incorruption, not, of course, for the honour of life, but to serve the long duration of punishment. But no voice can set forth, no speech can explain the power of this punishment and of that fire. For there is nothing among corruptible things that can be compared to incorruptible ones, whether good or evil. What will we do there, what will we answer? There will be nothing but gnashing of teeth, but wailing and weeping, and late penance, with help failing on every side and punishments growing stronger on every side; but no consolation at all. No one will meet our eyes there except only the ministers of punishment and the dreadful faces of the torturers. Yet we can not only escape these punishments, these torments, but also acquire eternal blessedness, if only we do penance for our evils.

CHAPTER XIX. How it is corrupted. Yet even then it was not wholly fruitless. Let this be read with caution. Do you see how great is the power of penance? Do you see how much merit conversion has restored? But penance is corrupted if someone is entangled again in the same evils for which he confesses. For, it says, one building and another destroying, what will they gain but toil? And he who is baptised after [touching] a dead body, and touches the dead again, what does he gain by his washing? So too the man who fasts for his sins, and falls again, and does the same things: who will hear his prayer? (Ecclus. 34:28, 30, 31). And again it says: Whoever turns back from justice to sin, the Lord casts him down to the sword. And as a dog, when it returns to its vomit, becomes hateful, so is the fool when he returns to his sin (Prov. 26:11). But now listen to what we say. It often happens that someone has through penance corrected many great things, and yet, among these good things which he corrected through penance, has also committed sins; and this is what most of all brings despair into the mind, because he seems here to have destroyed what he had built, and to have poured out all those labours in vain. And this is the thought which above all lays the weight of despair on the soul. But on the other hand one must consider that by which this most evil thought, hostile to our life, may be driven back: namely, that if those good things which we did, and that amendment which was sought through penance, had not existed and, like a counterweight, been able to withstand what has been brought in upon us by sin, there would have been nothing to prevent us from falling into the depth of evils. But as it is, like some strong breastplate, it did not allow the heavy and bitter javelin to penetrate to the vital organs, but broke the greatest force of the deadly weapon. For it is certain that he who carries with him there many good works and many bad works will have some refreshment in the very punishments; but as for him who has no good works and brings back with him a great abundance of bad ones, there is no need to say what awaits him. For there will without doubt be a weighing of good and bad, and each side as if placed on a scale. The side which sinks down, toward which the weight tips, will claim the worker for itself. If, then, the multitude of evil works prevails, it drags its worker down to Gehenna; but if the good works are greater, they will resist with the utmost force and fight against the evil ones, and will call their doer back to the land of the living even from the very border of Gehenna. If, then, most dear brothers, we are willing to consider these things more attentively, let us acquire remedies for ourselves for the day of need, so that when the day of judgement comes we may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may happily come with the just and those who fear God to the eternal rewards. Amen.
